title: The Army With No General
principle: The first defences do not know what they are fighting.

t: Something tries to get into you roughly every few seconds. You almost never notice.
You are under continuous attack — every breath, every meal, every surface you touch. The reason you rarely notice is not that the attacks are rare.
sub: So what is stopping all of it?
Most of the defending happens before anything clever gets involved.

question: What stops most germs getting into you?
What accounts for the majority of successful defence?
options: Walls and traps that do not know what they are stopping
The clever part of the immune system that recognises invaders
Nothing much — most germs are harmless
stages.outcome: Walls and traps that do not know what they are stopping
note: Have a guess before you look.
Commit. The clever part is famous, and it is not where most of the work happens.

t: Put each barrier next to what it does.
Each of these stops things without identifying them. Match them up.

label: A wall nothing can walk through
A physical barrier: dead, dry, and continuously shed
Sticky stuff that traps things
Traps particles and sweeps them out
A bath that kills most things you swallow
pH around 1.5 — lethal to most swallowed organisms
Making yourself too hot for them
Raises temperature past many pathogens' optimum

t: The first defences do not know what they are fighting. They stop nearly everything anyway.
This is innate immunity: fast, general, and completely uninterested in what it is stopping.
Innate immunity — barriers, phagocytes and inflammation — responds within minutes to broad classes of threat, using receptors for features shared by whole groups of pathogens.

It recognises patterns rather than individuals: bacterial cell-wall components, double-stranded RNA, flagellin. Those are features a pathogen cannot easily abandon, which is why a system with a few dozen receptors can cover an enormous range of threats and why it has changed little in hundreds of millions of years.
sub: No memory, no learning, and it does most of the work.
It never improves and never remembers, and it handles the overwhelming majority of encounters.
Plants and insects have only this, and it is entirely sufficient for them.
Adaptive immunity is the expensive addition, found only in vertebrates. That most of life manages without it is a good corrective to the assumption that the sophisticated part is the important part.

q: Does your skin know what it is keeping out?
Do innate defences identify what they are stopping?
On what basis does innate immunity discriminate?
options: No — it stops everything the same way
Only if you have met that germ before
why: Skin does not identify anything. It is a wall, and a wall works on whatever arrives. That is why it is so effective and why a burn or a cut is so dangerous.

Innate defences are non-specific. They act on broad features rather than identities, which is what lets them respond in minutes — and why breaching them, by a wound or a catheter, is such a common route to serious infection.

Pattern recognition rather than identification: receptors for conserved molecular features that pathogens cannot easily discard. This is the trade the system makes — speed and breadth for precision — and it is why the adaptive system exists to cover what gets through.

t: This is why a burn is so dangerous. The wall is gone.

Severe burns kill by infection more often than by the injury itself, because the largest barrier you have is missing over a wide area. It is also why hand-washing does more for hospital infection rates than any drug: most of defence is keeping things out, and most of transmission is putting them where they can get in.
